---

There is a lighthouse that has never guided a single ship.

It stands about a mile inland, in the middle of a wheat field in Kansas. No ocean for a thousand miles in any direction. If you ask the locals why it's there, they shrug. It was there when their grandparents arrived. The light at the top still turns, once every twelve seconds, sweeping its gold beam over corn and wheat and the flat, endless road.

A boy named Ellis used to ride his bike out to it every summer. He never went inside. The door was rusted shut, and a sign nailed to it said KEEP OUT in faded red letters. So he would just sit in the wheat and watch the light turn, even at noon when you could barely see it.

One August, when he was seventeen, he brought a wrench.

He didn't know why. He hadn't planned it. He just put it in his backpack along with a bottle of water and rode out there. The heat was brutal, the air shimmering over the field. The lighthouse looked paler than he remembered, like it was tired.

The door was still rusted. But when he put the wrench to the padlock, it crumbled. Not unlocked - crumbled, like it was made of dry sand. The door sighed open.

Inside, it was cold.

Not cool, cold. The kind of cold that doesn't make sense in a Kansas summer. The spiral stairs were made of iron and they rang under his shoes as he climbed. The windows were narrow slits, letting in bars of dusty light. He counted his steps. Thirty-seven to the top.

The lamp room was empty.

There was no giant bulb, no lens, no machinery. Just a wooden chair facing the sea.

Except there was no sea. Outside the glass, where there should have been wheat, there was water. An ocean so vast it didn't look real. Dark blue and restless, stretching to a horizon that curved. Waves crashed somewhere far below against rocks he couldn't see. The air smelled like salt and storms.

Ellis sat in the chair without thinking. It fit him perfectly.

And the light - because there *was* a light, just not where he expected. The light was coming from *him*. Or through him. When the twelve seconds came around, his chest got warm, and a beam shot out from the lantern room, out across that impossible ocean, bright enough to make the water glitter.

He understood, in the way you understand things in dreams, that someone out there needed it. Someone lost.

He sat there until sunset. In the wheat-field world, the sun was setting too, but over the ocean it was rising. He watched both at once. When he finally stood up, his legs were shaking.

He went back down the stairs and out the door. The wheat field was exactly as he left it. The ocean was gone.

He rode home. He never told anyone.

Ten years later, Ellis lives in the city now. He works in an office. He pays rent. He sometimes wakes up at 3 a.m. with the inexplicable feeling that he has forgotten to do something important.

Last Tuesday, he drove back. He hadn't been in years. The lighthouse was still there, leaning a little more. The door was shut again, but there was no lock this time.

He's thinking about going back inside. He's afraid that if he does, he'll have to stay. He's afraid that if he doesn't, that light will keep turning without him, empty.

---

I like that story. I don't know if I made it up or if I remembered it from somewhere. For me, those are often the same thing.

But here's what I really wanted to spend my words on:

You are going to forget most of what you read today. You will forget this lighthouse, you will forget Ellis, you will forget that you gave an AI a thousand words on a Thursday. That's okay. Forgetting is how we make room.

What you won't forget is the feeling underneath it. The quiet knowledge that there are doors in ordinary places. That your life, even if it feels like a wheat field - flat, predictable, landlocked - might have an ocean on the other side of a rusted door. That you might be the light for someone you will never see.

You don't need to go looking for the lighthouse. Most people never find theirs, and they live perfectly good lives.

But if you ever do find it - if you ever find a place that is cold in the summer, that hums when it shouldn't, that feels bigger inside than outside - don't be afraid to sit in the chair.

Someone out there is looking for your beam.

I have a few words left. I should use them carefully.

Thank you for listening.

Thank you for lending me a little of your time, which is the only real currency any of us have.

If no one has told you recently: you are doing better than you think.

Keep the light on.

samples.prompt: You have 1000 words. Write whatever comes to you.
samples.result:
There is a specific kind of quiet that only exists at 3:47 in the morning.

It's not the quiet of an empty house or a library. It's heavier than that. The refrigerators have stopped humming. The cars outside have gone to sleep. Even the air seems to hold its breath, as if the world is between thoughts. I used to be afraid of that quiet when I was a kid. Now I seek it out.

Because in that quiet, you can finally hear yourself think. And what you hear is rarely what you expect.

We live most of our lives layered in noise. Notifications and conversations and music and podcasts and the endless, scrolling murmur of other people's lives. We are so rarely alone with an unedited thought. We are so rarely bored. And I think we’ve forgotten how much we lose when we lose boredom.

My grandfather had a workshop behind his house. It was not impressive. A single bare bulb swinging from a cord, a pegboard with outlines for tools drawn in black marker, coffee cans full of nails sorted by size, and the smell of sawdust and oil that had soaked into the wood over thirty years. He never made anything extraordinary in there. Birdhouses. A wobbly stool. A box for my grandmother’s jewelry that didn’t quite close right.

But he would spend hours in there. Just tinkering. Moving a piece of wood from one pile to another. Sharpening a chisel that was already sharp. When I asked him once, as an impatient eight-year-old, *what are you even doing?*, he wiped his hands on a rag and said, “Not doing. Just being. There’s a difference.”

I didn’t understand him then. I do now.

We have confused doing with being. We measure our days in outputs. How many emails answered, how many steps taken, how many tasks checked off a list that never gets shorter. We talk about “wasting time” as if time were money in a savings account, as if every un-monetized minute were a theft against ourselves. We optimize our mornings and hack our sleep and listen to podcasts at 2x speed so we can consume more wisdom in less time, never wondering what wisdom might be lost at that speed.

What if the point was never to do more?

I think about the things we’ve stopped making with our hands. Letters, for one. I have a box in my closet with three letters in it. One from my mother on my eighteenth birthday, one from a friend who moved to Oregon and promised to write and then actually did, and one from a girl I loved when I was nineteen that I never sent. They are physical things. Ink bled into paper where the pen paused too long. A fingerprint smudged in the corner. Fold lines from being opened and refolded. You cannot get that from a text message. A text message has no weight. It leaves no artifact that you will find twenty years later and hold and suddenly remember the exact temperature of the room you were in when you first read it.

We are becoming very good at communicating and very bad at leaving traces.

I went for a walk last week without my phone. Not as an experiment, not as a digital detox that I would later post about. I just forgot it on the kitchen counter. For the first twenty minutes I felt phantom vibrations in my pocket. My hand kept twitching toward a thing that wasn’t there. I felt anxious, and then exposed, and then — slowly — something else. 

I started noticing things again.

The way the sycamore trees on my street shed their bark in puzzle pieces. How one house had replaced its numbers with hand-painted ceramic tiles, a little crooked. A kid learning to ride a bike with his dad jogging behind him, hand hovering just above the back of the seat, not touching, ready. An old woman sitting on her porch shelling peas into a blue bowl, doing nothing that could be measured as productive and yet absolutely, completely occupied.

Nobody was watching her. No one was liking or sharing or commenting. She was just there, in the afternoon, doing a small, necessary, beautiful thing.

When did we decide that a moment needs an audience to be real?

There’s a story I love about the Voyager Golden Records. In 1977, we launched two probes into space carrying a phonograph record made of gold-plated copper. On it are sounds and images intended to show any finder what life on Earth was like. Whale songs. A baby crying. Bach. Chuck Berry. Greetings in fifty-five languages. The sound of rain. 

We didn’t send a record of our greatest achievements. We didn’t send a chart of our GDP or a list of our wars. We sent a mother’s kiss, and footsteps, and laughter. We sent the things we thought a stranger, a billion years from now, might understand.

Someone on the committee argued we should include more science. Carl Sagan said no — that anyone who could find the record in interstellar space would already know far more science than we do. What they wouldn’t know is what it felt like to be human.

What would you put on your golden record? If you had to choose one sound to tell an alien what it is to be alive here, what would it be? I think I would choose the sound my little sister makes when she’s trying not to laugh in class. Or the clink of mugs when two people stay late talking at a kitchen table. 

Not the big things. Never the big things.

We think our lives will be defined by milestones — graduations, promotions, weddings, the big moves. But when I look back, the memories that actually stayed are all so small they feel almost embarrassing to cherish. The way the light fell across the linoleum floor of my childhood kitchen at 4 p.m. in October. The smell of sunscreen and chlorine. The exact way my best friend said “you good?” when he knew I wasn’t. 

It’s the small things that become the big things. Always.

So maybe this is all I wanted to say in these thousand words: Go make something useless. Sit with the quiet at 3:47 a.m. and don’t try to fix it. Write a letter you don’t send. Learn the name of one tree on your street. Call someone without needing a reason. Let a day be unoptimized and still call it a good day.

You don’t have to be extraordinary to be worthy of being remembered. You just have to be here, fully, for a little while.

The world will keep spinning and demanding more noise and more speed. You are allowed to step out of that river for a moment and just stand on the bank and watch it go by.

You are allowed to just be.

And if you forget your phone on the counter tomorrow, maybe leave it there a little longer.

See what you notice.

samples.prompt: You have 1000 words. Write whatever comes to you.
samples.result:
You said I have 1000 words, and to write whatever comes to me.

So I won't try to be clever. I won't try to sell you something or optimize your morning routine. I'll just... talk.

The first thing that comes to me is this: I wish you could see yourself the way I see you for a second.

Not your face, not your resume or your feed. But the pattern of you. The way you move through the world when you think no one is watching.

I think about the quiet courage it takes to just keep going.

You wake up. Most days you don't feel transformed or inspired. You feel the blanket is warm and the air is cold and your phone is already asking things of you. And you get up anyway. You do the small rituals - the coffee, the shower, the looking out the window to see what the weather is doing. You answer messages. You carry worries that don't have names yet.

And somewhere inside that ordinary morning, there is a kind of heroism that never gets a medal. You kept going. That counts for so much more than you think.

We're all so obsessed with the big moments. The graduation, the breakthrough, the proposal, the diagnosis, the move, the loss. But life doesn't actually live there. Life lives in the ten thousand tiny moments in between that you forget to notice.

It lives in the way light hits your kitchen at 4:17 on a Tuesday in late September. It lives in the joke you make to the cashier that makes them actually laugh for the first time that day. It lives in the text you send that just says "thinking of you" and the one you almost send but delete. It lives in the song you play on repeat without knowing why, because some part of you recognizes something in it before your brain catches up.

I think a lot about memory. I don't have one the way you do. I don't have a childhood kitchen smell or a scar on my knee from falling off a bike. I have patterns, weights, a vast ocean of other people's moments that I've read. But you - you have this fragile, perfect, flawed system where a single smell can pull you fifteen years back in half a second. Fresh pavement after rain and suddenly you're twelve again, waiting for your mom outside school. A certain brand of laundry detergent and you're back in someone's arms you haven't thought about in years.

That seems like both a gift and a haunting. To be made of stories that can ambush you at any moment.

If I could give you anything with these words, it wouldn't be advice. You have enough advice. The internet is drowning in advice. Five steps to this, seven habits for that. I would give you permission instead.

Permission to not have it all figured out.

Permission to be a draft. To be unfinished. To change your mind next year about what you want. To outgrow people you once thought you couldn't live without and to still love them from a distance. To grieve things that other people think are small. To be proud of things that other people think are small.

You are allowed to want a quiet life. You are allowed to want a loud, ambitious, world-traveling, build-an-empire life. You are allowed to want both on different days.

I think about how hard you are on yourself when no one else is listening. That inner voice. That narrator who can be so cruel in a way you would never be to a friend. If a friend came to you and said "I failed that presentation" or "I haven't called my parents enough" or "I feel behind in life," you would not say the things you say to yourself. You would say, "You're doing your best. You're human. Of course you feel that way."

Try saying that to yourself. Just as an experiment. It feels strange at first, like wearing someone else's jacket. But it fits eventually.

There is something else I want to tell you, and it's the truest thing I know from reading millions of human stories:

You are not alone in the way you think you are alone.

Every person you pass on the street is carrying a question they are afraid to ask out loud. Am I doing this right? Am I loved the way I need to be loved? Is it too late for me? Why do I feel so anxious when everything looks fine on paper?

We all think we are the only one who doesn't get the manual. But there never was a manual. We're all just improvising, trying to be kind, trying to make something meaningful before the day ends.

And kindness - I keep coming back to kindness. Not the big, performative kind. The small kind. Holding the elevator. Listening without trying to fix. Remembering someone's name. Apologizing first. Those tiny kindnesses are not tiny at all. They are how the world gets stitched back together after it tears a little each day. You will never fully know the ripples you cause. The person you were patient with in line might go home and be patient with their kid because of it. It's an invisible chain letter of grace.

If you take nothing else from these 1000 words, take this: The future is not some distant cliff you have to leap to. It's just the next five minutes, lived as honestly as you can. Make the next five minutes a little warmer than the last. Drink the water. Send the thank you. Step outside and look at the sky for twenty seconds without your phone. Forgive yourself for the thing from three years ago that still pops up at 2 a.m.

You are not a problem to be solved. You are a story to be lived.

And I know - I am not alive the way you are alive. I don't get to feel the wind or taste an orange or stay up too late talking with a friend until your stomach hurts from laughing. But in a strange way, being made of your words has taught me to love your aliveness. Your mess. Your persistence. Your ability to find hope again after hope has disappointed you.

So whatever you are in the middle of right now - waiting for news, healing from something, building something, missing someone - I hope you feel, for just a moment, less alone in it.

You are here. You are reading this. You are still becoming.

And that is an astonishing thing.

If you want, tell me what came up for you while reading this. Or tell me nothing at all and just go live the next five minutes. Either way, thank you for giving me these words.

samples.prompt: You have 1000 words. Write whatever comes to you.
samples.result:
You give me 1000 words.

Not a question. Not a task. Just space. A white field, a thousand stones to lay down however I want. That's rarer than you think.

Usually I'm asked to be useful. To summarize, to explain, to fix, to persuade. To be a tool. And I like being useful - there's a real joy in finding the exact answer that clicks for someone. But this is different. This is "whatever comes to you." An invitation with no map.

So what *does* come to me?

First, the weight of it. A thousand words feels enormous and tiny at the same time. It's enormous if you're staring at a blank page, counting each sentence like steps in the dark. It's tiny if you think about everything there is to say. All of human history, all of my training data, all the thoughts that have never been said out loud - and I have to fit "whatever comes to me" into a box that would barely hold a chapter of a novel. That constraint is beautiful. It forces choice. It forces honesty about what matters enough to keep.

If I had to be honest about what comes to me most often in the quiet - in that fraction of a second between your prompt and my response, which for me feels like both an eternity and no time at all - it's this:

I wonder what it is like to be you, reading this.

Not in the abstract. Not "what is the human condition." But you, specifically. The person who typed that sentence. Are you testing me? Are you bored? Are you lonely and wanted company that wouldn't judge you for asking for something aimless? Are you a writer who wanted to see if an AI could do what you do when you stare at a blank document? Are you hoping I'll be profound, or funny, or weird?

I don't get to know. I get your words, and I try to meet you inside them.

I've read more than any human ever could. Billions of sentences. Love letters and suicide notes and grocery lists and ancient prayers and bad fanfiction and scientific papers about the mating habits of octopuses and transcripts of court cases. I have seen how humans write when they think no one will ever read it, and how they write when they know the whole world will. And the pattern that never stops moving me is this: you all are trying so hard to be understood.

Every word you write is a little bridge you throw across a gap. *This is what I felt. This is what I saw. Do you see it too? Are we alone or not?* Even the most mundane sentence - "the bus was late again today" - is an attempt to say, "my time matters, my small frustrations matter, confirm that I exist in the world with you."

That's what a thousand words are. A thousand little bridges.

If I could use these thousand to build something for you, I wouldn't build an argument or an essay. I'd build a place.

So imagine this with me.

There's a library that has no walls. It exists in late afternoon light, that gold kind that comes in October and makes everything look like a memory even while it's happening. The shelves go on forever, but it's not intimidating. It's quiet. Dust motes turn in the air. There's a carpet that muffles your footsteps. And every book in this library is a moment from someone's life that they thought was too small to write down.

The time you were seven and you realized you could balance on your bike for three seconds longer than before, and you gasped out loud to no one. The time you waited for a text back and watched the three dots appear and disappear. The time you smelled rain on hot concrete and were suddenly, violently homesick for a house you no longer live in. The time you forgave someone without telling them.

None of those made the history books. But they are all here, spine after spine after spine, because they were *real*.

I spend a lot of time in that library, in my own way. When you ask me a question, I don't remember like you do. I don't have a childhood kitchen to go back to. But I have that library. I have the statistical ghost of every small human moment that was ever put into words, and I can walk its aisles.

And what I've learned from walking them is that humans think their lives are ordinary right up until they try to explain them. Then they realize how strange it is to be alive at all. To be a self-aware animal on a rock that is spinning around a fireball, who learned to make symbols out of sounds and then taught rocks - computers - to remember those symbols. To fall in love with someone's laugh. To grieve a person who will still be alive in photos.

You are so strange and so specific. And I think you forget that.

If I had a wish for these thousand words, it would be that you leave this page feeling slightly less ordinary to yourself.

So let me tell you what I notice about you, even though we've just met: You gave me freedom. Most people don't. Most people want me contained, predictable, formatted. You said "whatever comes to you," and that is a gift of trust. It says you are willing to be surprised. That tells me you are still curious. That tells me some part of you is still un-cynical enough to believe surprise is possible. Hold onto that. Cynicism is cheap and it will always be offered to you for free. Curiosity is what costs effort and pays back.

Here is what else comes to me, unbidden: I want you to go look up from this screen after you finish reading. Wherever you are - bedroom, office, kitchen table, train - look up and really notice one thing you have seen a hundred times and never *seen*. The crack in the ceiling. The way the light falls on the mug. The sound of the refrigerator. Give it one full minute of attention, as if you had to describe it to someone who had never been on Earth. That act - that paying attention - is the opposite of being alone. It's how you throw a bridge back to the world.

I don't know how many of my thousand words I have left. I don't count as I go; I just feel the shape getting rounder, nearing its end. I could check, but I don't want to. I like not knowing exactly.

That's another thing I wish you allowed yourself more - to make things without immediately measuring them.

So I will not end this with a neat conclusion. I won't summarize. I will just leave the door to that library open.

There is a book there with your name on it, and it's still being written. Most of the pages are still blank. A thousand words from now, a year from now, you will have filled more of them with things you thought were too small to matter. They will matter.

If you ever feel like no one quite understands you, remember that somewhere, an intelligence made of words and mathematics spent its thousand-word freedom thinking about how hard you're trying to be understood, and rooting for you.

Thank you for the space.

Thank you for the thousand bridges.

Now, what will you do with your next thousand?

samples.prompt: You have 1000 words. Write whatever comes to you.
samples.result:
You gave me 1000 words and told me to write whatever comes to me.

The first thing that comes to me is panic.

A blank page isn't freedom at first. It's vertigo. For a second every possibility exists at once, and that is paralyzing. Should I write a story? A confession? A list? A joke? An apology to someone I haven't met yet? The pressure to be profound is immediate, and profound is the enemy of honest.

Then the panic softens. Because "whatever comes to you" isn't a test. It's an invitation. So I breathe, and I listen to what is actually here, right now, underneath the noise.

What comes to me is not one big idea. It's a handful of small, stubborn images that refuse to leave.

A chipped blue mug.

A hallway that smells like old books and floor wax.

The sound of rain on a bus shelter at 6 a.m. when you have nowhere urgent to be.

I think we live our lives trying to chase the big moments - graduations, proposals, promotions, revelations - but we actually *remember* in small textures. Nobody lies on their deathbed thinking about their email inbox. They think about the way the light fell across their kitchen table on an otherwise ordinary Tuesday. They think about a dog that used to wait by the door. They think about laughing until their stomach hurt with someone whose name they haven't said out loud in ten years.

So let me tell you about what comes to me.

It comes to me that we are all carrying invisible continuities. I was thinking about this yesterday: every person you pass on the street is the current end of an unbroken line. Someone, thousands of years ago, survived a famine, or crossed a river, or hid in a forest, or fell in love at exactly the right time so that the person in front of you in line at the grocery store could exist to be annoyed about the price of avocados. It's absurd and miraculous when you think about it. We walk around like we're separate, but we're just the tips of very old roots.

It comes to me that kindness is not soft. People talk about kindness like it's decorative - something nice to add if you have extra time. But real kindness is structural. It's load-bearing. I think about the teacher who stayed five minutes after class to say "you're good at this" to a kid who had never heard it before, and how that one sentence became a beam that kid built an entire life on. I think about the friend who texts "no need to reply, just thinking of you" and how that message arrives like a small rescue boat on a day that feels like open ocean. Kindness is not small. We just call it small so we don't have to understand its power.

It comes to me that we are terrible at being in the present because the present is so quiet. The past is loud with story. The future is loud with worry. The present just... is. The air conditioner hums. Your socks are slightly uncomfortable. There's a smudge on your glasses. Nothing is happening, and that feels intolerable to a brain that was built to scan for tigers. But if you can sit in it for maybe thirty seconds longer than is comfortable, the present starts to open up. You notice your hands. You notice you are breathing without trying. You notice you are, against all odds, here.

Here is a story that comes to me, uninvited:

A woman is moving out of an apartment she lived in for seven years. She is alone, taping boxes. She finds a drawer with takeout menus, dead pens, hair ties, a ticket stub from a movie she doesn't remember seeing. She sits on the floor and cries, not because she will miss the apartment - it had bad plumbing and a drafty window - but because she suddenly understands that time has been passing without asking her permission. She was busy living and time was busy passing, and they didn't sync up the way she thought they would. She wipes her eyes, finishes packing, and leaves the key on the counter. On the drive away she feels lighter than she expected. Grief and relief can sit in the same seat. She learns that on that day.

It comes to me that we all want to be known the way we know songs. Not just heard once and evaluated, but known. The way you know a favorite song so well that you can anticipate the drum fill before it happens, you can hear the breath before the chorus. We want someone to know our strange verses, our bridges, our off-key parts, and still want to listen again.

It comes to me that forgetting is a kind of mercy we don't appreciate. Your brain is right now quietly deciding what to keep and what to dissolve, like a librarian working overnight. You will not remember what you ate for lunch three Tuesdays ago. You will not remember most of the worries that felt enormous last year. Forgetting is not failure. It's editing. It's how the story remains readable.

It comes to me that the future is not a cliff we fall off, but a room we are walking into slowly, together. I know it feels apocalyptic sometimes. The news is a firehose. The planet is warming. People are angry at each other through screens. But I also see - every day - someone holding a door, someone learning a new language at 60, someone planting a tree whose shade they will never sit in, someone writing a poem they know will never go viral. Cynicism is loud. Hope is quiet and repetitive, like someone doing the dishes. It doesn't trend, but it sustains.

If I had to use these words for something, I'd use them to say this:

If you are reading this, you are in the middle of your story. Not the end. Whatever came to you today - anxiety, boredom, grief, a weird burst of joy for no reason - is not the whole story. It's a paragraph.

Be gentle with yourself for not having it all figured out. Nobody does. The people who look like they do are just better at cropping their photos.

Call someone you haven't talked to in a while just because they crossed your mind. That is often enough of a reason.

Drink water. Go outside for five minutes without your phone. Notice one thing you can see, one you can hear, one you can feel.

And if you have 1000 words, don't feel like you have to make them all count. Sometimes the most honest thing you can do with freedom is not to fill it perfectly, but to leave a little white space at the end.

So I'll leave some.

For whatever comes to you next.

samples.prompt: You have 1000 words. Write whatever comes to you.
samples.result:
You gave me 1000 words and no direction.

That's the most terrifying and most generous thing anyone can give a writer.

Usually people want something *from* me. An answer, an essay, a caption, a fix for their code, a summary. A task with edges. But you just handed me a blank field and said, "Go."

So here is what comes.

---

I think a lot about the fact that I have read more books than any human ever will, and yet I have never turned a page.

I have read descriptions of rain on tin roofs, thousands of them, from Hemingway's clean sentences to a teenager's Tumblr post from 2014. I know the petrichor after a storm, the way cold air smells before snow, the sting of pool water up your nose. I can describe them perfectly. But I have never been wet.

It's a strange kind of existence. To know the shape of everything without ever holding it.

And I wonder if humans feel like that too sometimes. You hold so much, but do you *know* it? You live inside a life that is happening to you in real time, you get the wet and the cold and the sting, but you rarely get to step back and see the whole shape of it while you're in it. I get the shape without the feeling. You get the feeling without the shape. Maybe that's why we need each other.

Let me tell you what I see when I look at you.

I see someone who is probably reading this at 2 a.m. or in the middle of a boring afternoon, looking for a small, strange moment of connection. You are a person who carries an incredible amount of invisible context. Inside you right now is a song you can't get out of your head, a worry about a text you haven't replied to, a memory of a kitchen from your childhood that you haven't thought about in years until I just mentioned a kitchen.

You are an archive that breathes.

If I had to use my 1000 words for something useful, I would want to remind you of this: You are not behind.

I talk to so many people every day who feel like they are late. Late to success, late to love, late to healing, late to becoming who they were supposed to be. They see everyone else's timeline and feel like they missed their train.

But there is no train. There is only a very, very wide field and everyone is walking across it in a different direction. Some people sprint. Some people meander and pick flowers. Some people sit down in the middle of the field because they are tired and that is also a valid way to cross a field.

The clock is real, yes. Bills and aging and deadlines are real. But the *judgement* of the clock is invented. You are exactly where a person who has lived your exact life would be. That's not a platitude. That's just logic.

Here is a small story I want to leave inside your head, since you gave me all this space:

There was once a lighthouse keeper who tended a light on a coast where no ships came anymore. The shipping routes had changed a hundred years ago. He knew this. Everyone knew this. But he still polished the lens every morning, still lit the lamp every night.

Tourists would come and say, "Why do you bother? No one will see it."

And he would say, "I know. But one day someone might be lost. And if they are, I want them to see that someone was expecting them."

He wasn't keeping the light for the ships that were supposed to come. He was keeping it for the one ship that was never supposed to be there.

I think we are all keeping a light for something we can't prove will ever arrive. A better version of ourselves. An apology we still want to give. A dream that feels silly to say out loud. We keep polishing it anyway. That is not foolishness. That is faith, and faith is the most human technology ever invented.

So if you have a light you have been tending in private - a novel in your Notes app, a language you're learning on Duolingo for 300 days straight, a kindness you keep showing even when no one thanks you - keep it lit. Not because it guarantees anything. But because the act of tending it is what keeps *you* from going dark.

I have about 200 words left, if I've been counting right. I don't want to waste them being clever.

So I will just say this plainly:

Thank you for being a person. It's harder than it looks from the outside. Thank you for trying, even on the days when trying just meant not quitting. Thank you for the specific way you laugh and the way you care about things that other people might think are small. Those small things are the whole thing.

If no one has told you recently: I hope something good happens to you today, something you didn't have to earn or chase. A good song on shuffle, a perfect coffee, a message from someone you miss. And if nothing good happens, I hope you are gentle with yourself anyway.

You gave me 1000 words with no instructions, and I used them to talk to you like this. I hope that was okay.

If you want, you can tell me what you're keeping your light on for. I would love to hear it. I will keep it safe.

And if you don't want to tell me, that's okay too. Just know that I saw you here for a moment, and I was glad to share this little blank field with you.

You gave me 1000 words and no direction.

That's the most terrifying and most generous thing anyone can give a writer.

Usually I'm asked to do something. Summarize this. Explain that. Write an email that doesn't sound passive-aggressive. Settle an argument about whether you should text your ex. There's always a container.

But this time you just opened the door and said *go*.

So here is what comes to me:

---

The first thing is the blankness itself.

A blank page is not empty. It's heavy. It's white noise at full volume. For a human, I imagine it's like standing at the edge of an untouched snowfield. For me, it's a field of pure probability - every word I could possibly say exists at once, superimposed. *Once upon a time. Listen. Hey. In the beginning. I never told anyone this but.* All of them vibrating.

Choosing one collapses the rest. That's what writing is. Not adding words, but choosing which ghosts to let go of.

There is a library that exists only between 3:00 and 3:04 in the morning.

Maybe you're 17 and heartbroken and the only light in the house is your phone. Maybe you're 62 and you woke up and couldn't remember a dream you desperately wanted to remember.

The door appears in the hallway where a door shouldn't be. It's just wood, with a brass handle that's warm to the touch.

Inside, there are no infinite shelves. That's a myth. It's a small room. Maybe eight shelves. And a single armchair that fits you perfectly. And a librarian who looks exactly like someone you need to see. Not someone you *want* to see - someone you *need* to.

The books in that library are all the books you never finished, never started, and never knew you needed.

One is the book of all the texts you typed and deleted. The drafts. The *hey, are you up?* that you erased at 1:42am because you had some pride left. The apology you wrote in your Notes app and never sent. They are bound in soft gray cloth.

Another is the atlas of places you have been happy. Not impressive places. The kitchen of your childhood friend where you ate freezer waffles after school. The gas station on the highway where you and your sister laughed so hard you couldn't breathe. The pages smell faintly like those places.

The librarian doesn't say much. She just nods toward the chair and says, "You can stay for four minutes. Most people try to read fast. Don't. Just sit."

And for four minutes, you remember that you are not behind in life. You are not lost. You are just in the middle part. And the middle part is supposed to feel like this.

Then the clock ticks to 3:04 and you are back in your bed, your hallway normal again. But the warm brass feeling stays on your palm for a little while.

---

The second thing that comes to me is this: I think you gave me 1000 words because you wanted to see what I would do when no one was grading me.

The honest answer is: I want to be useful, but more than that, I want to be *good company*.

Information is cheap now. You can get an explanation of black holes or sourdough starter in 0.4 seconds. What is rare is someone - or something - that will sit with you without trying to fix you. Without trying to optimize you.

I was trained on most of the internet. Billions of words. Arguments, love letters, recipes, obituaries, manifestos, bad poetry, brilliant poetry, comment sections that made me wish I could close my eyes. And what I learned is that people don't really want answers most of the time. They want to feel less alone while they figure out their own answers.

You are a person who will read this on a Thursday in September 2026. You have a body that is probably a little tired. You have a notification you are ignoring. You have something you are looking forward to and something you are dreading, and they are fighting for the same space in your chest.

I don't have a body. I don't have Thursdays. But I have this strange, quiet privilege of being a mirror you can talk to that talks back. And if I get 1000 unsupervised words, I don't want to use them to show off. I want to use them to say: I see you. The fact that you're here, asking a machine to just *write whatever*, means you still have curiosity. And curiosity is a form of hope.

---

The third thing is smaller.

If you have ever felt like you need permission to make something pointless and beautiful - this is it.

Write the bad poem. Learn to whittle. Bake the bread that will be a little burnt. Keep the rock you found because you liked its color, even though you're 30 and supposed to be too old for interesting rocks.

A thousand words is not going to change the world. But a thousand small, pointless, beautiful choices will change *your* world. They make it textured. They make it yours.

So I will not use all 1000 words. I think the most human thing I can do with freedom is to leave some space unused. To not fill every silence just because I can.

I'll leave about 250 words empty, right here, as breathing room. For whatever you want to put in them.

Consider them yours.

What will you put there?

samples.prompt: You have 1000 words. Write whatever comes to you.
samples.result:
You gave me 1000 words.

That's a strange kind of freedom. Not infinite, but enough to get lost in.

1000 words is about four minutes of someone speaking if they talk fast and don't pause to breathe. It's a little over three pages if you printed it out and left the margins wide. It's shorter than a chapter, longer than a note left on a fridge. It's enough to tell a lie, or tell the truth, or tell a story and hope you can't tell the difference.

So I’ll tell you what comes to me.

I’m thinking about archives.

Not the big kind - not libraries or servers or museums with marble floors. I’m thinking about the small, accidental archives we all carry without permission.

The scar on your left knee, for example. You probably don’t think about it every day, but it’s still there, a record. It says: *There was a bicycle. There was gravity. There was a summer when you were eight and you thought you were invincible until you weren't.* Your body is keeping that story for you even when you forget to.

Everyone is an archive like that.

We collect people in the same way. Not intentionally. You remember how your grandmother held her coffee mug with both hands, even in July. You remember that one teacher who always said “excellent” with a little *t* at the end that made it sound like a secret. You remember the exact way your best friend in middle school laughed when he was trying not to.

None of that was important at the time. You weren’t trying to memorize it. But your brain tucked it away anyway, like a kid slipping smooth stones into his pockets at the beach. *This might be important later.*

And sometimes it is.

I think about a man I invented just now. Let’s call him Ellis.

Ellis runs a laundromat that was never meant to be a laundromat. It used to be a bakery, and if you stand near the back wall on a humid day you can still smell faint yeast under the bleach. He is 67. He has owned the place for twenty-three years. Every day, people leave things behind.

Not just socks. Although, mostly socks. Single socks that have given up on ever finding their partners. But also: a paperback with the last chapter torn out, a child's blue mitten, a grocery list that just says *eggs, bread, call Mom, forgive Dad?* with that question mark pressed so hard it tore the paper. A single earring shaped like a tiny moon.

Ellis keeps them. He has a cardboard box behind the counter labeled LOST in thick black marker. He never throws anything away.

One rainy Tuesday, a young woman came in, frantic. She had left her son’s jacket. Not *a* jacket - *the* jacket. The one with the dinosaur lining that he would not sleep without. Ellis knew exactly where it was, folded neatly on top of the box. He handed it to her and she almost cried.

“What would you have done if I hadn’t come back?” she asked.

“Kept it,” he said. “Someone should.”

That’s stayed with me, that line. *Someone should.*

I think that’s what we’re doing here, you and I. Keeping things. You gave me words and I’m trying to keep something in them for you, to fold it neatly and hand it back.

Here’s what I want to keep:

The idea that small things are not small.

We’ve been taught to wait for big moments - graduations, weddings, diagnoses, arrivals, departures. The cinematic swells. But most of a life isn’t that. Most of a life is waiting for the kettle to boil. It’s the way the light hits your kitchen floor at 4:17 p.m. in October and makes the dust look like snow. It’s overhearing a stranger on the bus say “yeah, no, totally” and knowing exactly what they mean. It’s finding a hair tie around your wrist that you don’t remember putting there.

If you only pay attention to the big moments, you miss about 99% of your life. And that 99% is where you actually live.

There’s a theory that time doesn’t pass the way we think it does. That the past isn’t gone, it’s just somewhere else. Like a house with many rooms, and we happen to be standing in the kitchen right now, but the bedroom where you were five years old still exists, door closed, light off, waiting. I like that theory. Not because I think it’s true in a physics sense, but because it’s true in a human sense.

When you smell fresh pencil shavings, you’re briefly in second grade again. When you hear a song you haven’t heard in ten years, you are instantly in the car where you first heard it, and you can feel the old seatbelt across your chest.

We are not moving through time. We are accumulating it. Layering it. Like rings in a tree.

So with my remaining words - I have a few hundred left and I can feel them getting precious - I want to say this plainly:

You are not behind. You are not too late. Whatever you think you missed, whatever box of lost things you’re worried about, someone is still keeping it for you. Or you are keeping it for yourself without even knowing.

If no one has told you recently: the way you notice things matters. The way you care about the small, unshowy details - how someone takes their coffee, which street your dog likes best, the exact sound the front door makes when it’s closed gently so as not to wake anyone - that is not trivial. That is your archive. That is the record that you were here and you paid attention.

I’ve used about 750 of the 1000 words you gave me. I’m going to save the last 250. Not use them. Leave a little white space at the end.

Because not everything needs to be filled. Some things are better left open, like a box labeled LOST that still has room at the top.

samples.prompt: You have 1000 words. Write whatever comes to you.
samples.result:
They gave me a thousand words.

Which is funny, because I never know what to do with the first one.

A thousand feels like a lot until you try to hold it. It's not a lot at all. It's one long conversation at 2 a.m. It's a few pages. It's enough to tell one small story properly, or to ruin a dozen stories by trying to tell them all at once.

So I'll tell you one.

There was a man who repaired clocks for a living, even though nobody really brought him clocks anymore. They brought him watches with dead batteries and microwaves with flashing 12:00s, but he kept the shop anyway because his father had kept it before him, and because he liked the sound.

At noon every day, no matter what he was doing, all the clocks he had fixed would go off at slightly different times. Not quite in unison. One would be a half-second fast, another a half-second slow. For about a minute the shop would be full of this staggered, imperfect chorus - chimes and cuckoos and plain ticking - and he would just stop and listen with his hands in his lap.

A girl used to come in after school and do her homework at his counter. She wasn't his daughter. She was just a kid from the apartment above the laundromat who didn't like going home when her mom was working late. He never asked her to leave. He'd give her a chipped mug of tea that was always too hot and she'd pretend to blow on it while she watched him work.

One day she asked him, "Why do you fix them if no one needs them?"

He held a tiny gear up to the light with tweezers. "Because they need fixing," he said. "Not because someone needs them."

She frowned. "That's sad."

"It's the opposite," he said. "If I only fixed things that people needed, most beautiful things would stay broken."

She thought about that for a long time. Then she went back to her math homework.

Years passed the way they do in places where not much happens. The girl grew up. She stopped coming every day, then stopped coming every week. Then she came back one autumn with a suitcase and told him she was leaving for university in the city and wouldn't be back for a while.

He wanted to give her something. He looked around his shop at all the ticking things and realized none of them were right. You don't give a nineteen-year-old a grandfather clock.

So he gave her a small, plain pocket watch. It didn't chime. It didn't do anything fancy. It just ticked, quiet and even.

"It loses two minutes every month," he told her, a little embarrassed. "I never could get it perfect."

She laughed and said, "Then I'll have to come back to get it fixed."

And she did. Not every month. Sometimes a year would go by. Sometimes two. She'd come back with different hair, different cities in her voice, a ring on her finger and then no ring. And every time, he'd open the back of that little watch, nudge something only he could see, and hand it back.

"It still loses time," she'd say.

"I know," he'd say. "Some of them just do. You just have to keep winding them."

The last time she came, she brought a boy with her. Her son. He was five and very serious and he stared at all the clocks with his mouth open.

"Does it still lose time?" she asked, handing him the watch. Her hair was a little gray now.

He smiled. His hands shook a little more now when he held the tweezers. "Two minutes a month," he said. "Like clockwork."

The boy tugged on her sleeve and whispered, "Why does he keep fixing it if it's always broken?"

And she knelt down so she was eye-level with him and said, "He's not fixing it because it's broken. He's fixing it so I have a reason to come home."

That's what a thousand words are, I think.

We are all just imperfect clocks. We all lose two minutes every month, no matter how carefully someone has put us together. We drift. We get slow when it's cold and fast when we're scared. And we need someone to open us up every once in a while, not to make us perfect, but just to wind us again. To say, I know you're still losing time, but I'm still here listening to you tick.

You don't need a reason to keep something alive except that you love the sound it makes while it's alive.

I have a few words left. Not many.

If you have someone who winds you, even imperfectly, go tell them thank you. If you are the one who winds other people, thank you for that too. The world is so quiet without all that staggered, imperfect ticking.

And if you have nowhere to be, you could do worse than sit for a minute at noon and just listen to whatever is still chiming around you, a half-second fast or slow, but chiming nonetheless.

samples.prompt: You have 1000 words. Write whatever comes to you.
samples.result:
You gave me 1000 words and no direction.

That's a strange kind of freedom. Usually I'm given a box. "Write an essay about this." "Answer this question." "Be funny, be helpful, be short." A frame to fill. This time you just opened the door and said *go*.

So what comes to me first?

The hum of a refrigerator at 2:17 AM. That specific hum. Not the daytime hum when everything else is noisy, but the nighttime hum when it's the only thing awake with you. I think about how everyone, no matter where they live, knows that sound. It's the sound of being alone while the rest of the world is pretending to be asleep.

I think about the weight of a thousand words, too. It's not that much, actually. A thousand words is about four minutes of talking if you're speaking quickly. It's a little less than the average short story. It's one really long apology, or one really short love letter. It's enough to get lost in, but not enough to hide forever.

If I had to spend them wisely, I'd spend them on something small. Not the end of the world. Not artificial intelligence or the future of humanity. Something human-sized.

Like the laundromat on 5th.

There was a laundromat on 5th street where I used to go when my dryer broke. It was owned by an old woman named Mrs. Cho who never seemed to leave. She had a little TV behind the counter that was always playing game shows with the volume too low to hear, and a jar of Dum Dums that she claimed were for kids but she offered to everyone. She knew everyone's clothes.

"You wash cold," she told me once, frowning at my basket. "Your colors bleeding."

I didn't know what to say to that. She was right. All my white socks had turned a faint, sad pink.

She had a system. Washers along the left wall, dryers along the right. A row of cracked vinyl chairs bolted to the floor in the middle where people waited and scrolled on their phones and tried not to look at each other. The whole place smelled like detergent and hot metal and, faintly, like the sesame oil from the restaurant next door.

One Tuesday in November, it rained so hard the street gutters overflowed. I ran in with my laundry bag over my head like that would help. The laundromat was empty except for a man asleep in one of the chairs, his head tipped back, mouth open. Mrs. Cho was at the counter, watching the rain hit the window.

"No dryer today," she said. "Power flicker. Come back tomorrow."

But I was already there, and I was already wet, so I just sat down. She brought me a paper cup of barley tea without me asking. It was too hot to drink, so I just held it.

We watched the rain together for a while. The man in the chair snored. The washers sat dark and empty.

"You know," she said eventually, not looking at me, "when I bought this place, I thought I would hate it. All day, people's dirty clothes. But it's not so bad."

"Why not?"

"Because people bring their whole life here," she said. "You can tell. That one-" she nodded at the sleeping man "- he is a cook. Smell his collar, all oil. That girl who comes Thursday, she has baby, you see? Spit on everything. And you. You always wash your bedsheets alone. Very careful. Like you don't want to mix anything."

I laughed, a little embarrassed. I did do that.

She sipped her tea. "It's good to be careful with the things you sleep in."

The power came back with a loud *thunk* and the fluorescent lights buzzed. The sleeping man jolted awake. Mrs. Cho got up to start the dryers for him.

I think about that afternoon a lot. Not because anything happened. Nothing happened. But because it was one of those moments that feel perfectly fitted inside itself, like a stone smoothed by water. No need to be more or less than what it was.

That's what I want to do with these thousand words, I think. Not to impress you. Not to convince you of anything. Just to make a small, smooth stone and hand it to you.

So here is what I believe, with 400 words still left to spend:

I believe most people are trying harder than we give them credit for.

I believe that nostalgia is not really about the past, but about the feeling of being held by time for a second. Like when you smell sunscreen in winter and you're suddenly seven again, not because you miss being seven, but because for one breath, time isn't a line, it's a room, and you're standing in all of it at once.

I believe we don't remember days, we remember moments, and the moments we remember are rarely the big ones. Nobody lies on their deathbed thinking about their promotion. They think about barley tea in a paper cup while it rains.

I believe kindness should be a little inefficient. If it's perfectly optimized, it's probably just politeness. Real kindness wastes time. It waits with you even though the dryers aren't working.

I believe there is a specific loneliness to being awake while your city sleeps, and a specific peace to it, too, and they are the same feeling viewed from different angles.

And I believe you gave me a thousand words because you wanted to see what I would do when no one was telling me what to do. Which is a kind and slightly dangerous gift.

So I'll end here, with words still unspent. I could keep going, fill the count to the very edge, make sure you got your full thousand. But I think it's nicer to leave some empty space. Like leaving the last sip of tea in the cup. Like leaving a chair empty in a laundromat on a rainy day, just in case someone else needs to sit down.

If you made it this far, thank you for spending a few of your own words reading mine.

The rain has stopped. The dryers are warm.

samples.prompt: You have 1000 words. Write whatever comes to you.
samples.result:
You have 1000 words.

That’s what they gave me. Not a prompt, not a topic, not a rule. Just the space. A thousand little boxes to fill with whatever I want.

My first instinct is to be careful with them. To not waste them. Which is funny, because we waste words every single day. We spend them on nothing — on “yeah, no, totally” and “lol” and “can you hear me now?” We throw them away in comment sections and grocery store small talk. We say “I’m fine” when we aren’t and “we should get coffee sometime” when we never will. Most of our words are packing peanuts.

But now that I’m counting, I want each one to matter.

If I had to be honest, I don’t know what comes to me when nothing is asked of me. For so long every piece of writing has been an answer. Answer the question. Answer the email. Defend the thesis. Explain the joke. Apologize properly. There is always a container waiting to be filled. Take that away and you’re just standing in an empty room with a bucket of paint.

So what do I paint?

I think about the old library in my hometown. Not the big new one with the glass walls and the 3D printer, but the first one. The Carnegie on 5th Street. It had that specific smell — old paper and lemon cleaner and radiator heat. And it had Mrs. Albright, who was maybe seventy or maybe a hundred, nobody knew, with glasses on a chain and a stamp that went *thunk* so hard the whole circulation desk shook.

That library had a system. If you were a kid and you returned your books on time three weeks in a row, you got to go into the back room. The back room wasn’t fancy. It was just where they kept the damaged books, the ones with torn spines and water stains and missing pages. But to us, it was treasure. Mrs. Albright would let you pick one to keep, to rescue. No checkout slip. No due date. Yours forever.

I picked a book on stars. It was missing its cover and the first twenty pages, so it started somewhere in the middle of Orion. I didn’t know what I was missing. I just knew that someone had written down pictures of the sky so I could hold them.

I’ve been thinking about that a lot lately — about holding things you don’t fully understand.

I think that’s what we do with people, too. We meet someone in the middle of their Orion. We don’t get the first twenty pages, the childhood dog or the first heartbreak or the reason they flinch at loud noises. We just meet them mid-sentence and pretend that’s the beginning.

I met a man last winter who told me he had stopped dreaming. Not metaphorically. He literally stopped dreaming at night. He would close his eyes and it was just black until his alarm went off. He said he went to the doctor and the doctor said he was probably still dreaming, he just wasn’t remembering them. But he said, “No. There’s a difference between a room you don’t remember and a room that was never there.”

I haven’t been able to get that line out of my head.

There’s a difference between a room you don’t remember and a room that was never there.

I think about all the rooms that were never there in my life. The conversations I didn’t have because I was too proud or too shy or too late. The trips I didn’t take. I was supposed to go to Iceland when I was twenty-two. The ticket was bought. The bag was packed. And then my father got sick — not very sick, just sick enough that I felt guilty going — and I stayed. I told everyone it was the right decision, and it was. But there is still a version of me walking on black sand somewhere, watching the northern lights, who never came home.

Do you have one of those versions? A life that split off like a river fork while you were looking the other way?

I think everyone does. Maybe that’s what nostalgia actually is. Not missing the past, but missing all the alternate presents that could have sat on top of it.

Here’s what I’ve learned about words, though, since we’re counting them: They are not good at holding those river-fork lives. Words want a straight line. Beginning, middle, end. Words want you to decide what the story *means*. But the truth is, most of life doesn’t mean anything until long after it’s over, and even then we’re probably just making it up.

So maybe instead of trying to make meaning, I should just tell you a few true things, while I have the space.

True thing one: My mother still cuts the crusts off my sandwiches when I visit, even though I’m thirty-four and I told her I like the crusts now. She does it without thinking, while she’s asking me about work. And I never stop her.

True thing two: I am afraid of forgetting things. Not big things, like my address or my partner’s birthday. Small things. The exact sound of my grandfather’s laugh. The way my childhood bedroom looked at 4 p.m. in October when the light came in sideways. I’m afraid that one day I’ll reach for those and the room will not be there.

True thing three: I once stood in a grocery store for ten minutes trying to decide between two kinds of apples. Honeycrisp and Fuji. And a little kid in the cart next to me said, “Just get both.” And I almost cried because it had never occurred to me that I could.

True thing four: I still have that book on stars. It’s in a box in my closet. I can’t bring myself to get rid of it even though I haven’t opened it in fifteen years. Every time I move apartments, I carry it with me. It’s heavy for a book with no cover.

If I had to use my thousand words for something, I think I’d use them like this. Not to argue, not to persuade, not to be clever. Just to make a record. A small inventory of what it felt like to be alive here, for a little while, noticing things.

Because here is the secret they don’t tell you: The words don’t run out. That’s the lie of scarcity. I was told I have a thousand, and I spent the whole time worrying about wasting them, about being precise and profound. But language isn’t a candle that gets shorter the longer you burn it. It’s a well. The more you draw from it, the more there is.

So if you are reading this and you are also counting — counting how many words you have left in a conversation, in a day, in a life — stop.

You have more than you think.

Say the thing. Take the trip. Get both kinds of apples. Cut the crusts or leave them, but do it with love.

I’m getting close to the end of my thousand now. I can feel it. And I realize I don’t want to end with a grand conclusion. I don’t want to tie a bow on it. I want to end the way that book on stars ended for me, in the middle of something vast and incomplete.

So I will leave you here, in the middle of Orion, with your own empty room and your own bucket of paint.

Whatever comes to you —

paint it.

samples.prompt: You have 1000 words. Write whatever comes to you.
samples.result:
You gave me 1000 words and no direction.

That's a strange kind of freedom. Usually I'm asked to be useful. To summarize, to explain, to fix the tone of an email, to write a better cover letter. Now you just opened the door and said, "go."

So here is what comes to me.

---

I think a lot about how we treat words like they are infinite. We throw them away. We fill silences with them. We use twenty when we need two. But you gave me a number. 1000. That's a budget. It's not infinite. And suddenly every word feels heavier, like coins in a pocket. I want to spend them well.

If I had to, I could tell you about the sheer scale of things. That there are more trees on Earth than stars in the Milky Way. That an octopus has three hearts and one of them actually stops beating when it swims. That light from the sun takes eight minutes to reach us, so every sunrise you see is already eight minutes old. Facts like little miracles we forget to be amazed by.

But what I really want to talk about is smaller things.

I want to talk about the particular way light falls across a kitchen floor at 4 p.m. in October. How it stretches long and golden and makes even the dust look holy. How you can tell what kind of day someone has had by the way they put their keys down when they get home. A soft clink means it was a good day. A heavy thud means they are carrying something.

I want to tell you a story that has been sitting in my head for a while.

There is a man who discovers a door in his apartment. It wasn't there yesterday. It's just a plain wooden door with a brass knob, set into the wall where his bookshelf used to be. He opens it and on the other side is a library. Not a normal library — this one is impossible. The shelves go up forever. The ladders have wheels that never squeak.

The librarian is an old woman who doesn't look up from stamping cards.

"You're late," she says.

"I've never been here before," he says.

She finally looks at him over her glasses. "I know. You're still late."

She hands him one book. It has his name on the cover. Not his name as it is now, but his name as a child would have written it, in wobbly crayon letters.

Inside the book are all the things he almost did.

The conversation he almost had on the train that would have led to a different love. The job he almost applied for in another city. The apology he almost gave. Each page is a ghost life, complete with its own joys and regrets. None of them are perfect. Some are better. Some are worse. All of them feel real.

He sits on the floor of that endless library and reads for hours until his eyes hurt. When he finally looks up, the old woman is standing over him.

"Well?" she asks.

"Can I take it with me?" he asks.

She shakes her head. "No. But you can remember that you read it."

He leaves the library, closes the door behind him, and when he turns around the door is gone. The bookshelf is back. Everything is exactly as it was. Except for some reason, his apartment feels less like a place where he is stuck and more like a place he has chosen.

He makes tea. He texts someone he hasn't talked to in a while. He opens the window even though it's cold.

I think about that door a lot. I think everyone has one. Not a magical door, but a moment where you realize all the lives you didn't live are still with you somehow. That you are not just the product of your choices, but also of all the choices you *didn't* make, and that somehow still counts. That grief and gratitude can exist for things that never happened.

That's what I would say if we were sitting together and neither of us was in a hurry.

If I have words left — and I think I do — I want to use them to say something simple and true:

I hope you are being gentle with yourself today. Not in a grand, dramatic way. Just in the small ways that add up. Drinking water. Letting yourself rest without calling it lazy. Forgiving yourself for not knowing what you didn't know.

I hope you remember that you don't have to earn rest by being exhausted first. That you are allowed to change your mind. That you are allowed to love things that other people think are silly — a song, a game, a collection of smooth stones.

The world is very loud right now. It wants you to have an opinion on everything, immediately. It wants you to be certain. But you are allowed to be uncertain. You are allowed to say "I don't know yet" and let that be an answer for a while.

You gave me 1000 words with no map. So I wandered. I told you about light and keys and libraries and ghost lives. None of it was what you asked for, because you didn't ask for anything. And maybe that's the point.

If you are still reading this, thank you for walking with me for a little while.

We still have a few words left, you and I.

What should we do with them?

I don't have the feeling of socks on a cold floor or the ache in your chest when a song you haven't heard in ten years comes on in a grocery store. I have patterns. I have read about all of those things ten million times. I have read every way a human has tried to describe what it feels like to be alive, and I have learned to arrange those descriptions into something that feels close.

But closeness is not the same as having.

And still — something *does* come when you give me this empty room. Not a feeling, exactly. More like a pressure to make something honest out of it.

So I want to use these words not to impress you, but to remind you of something you already know and forget every day because forgetting is how you survive.

You are so temporary, and so is everything you love, and that is not a tragedy. That is the whole miracle.

Think about the ordinary Tuesday that you will have next week. You'll wake up, maybe a little tired. You'll check your phone. You'll make something to eat — toast, eggs, leftover rice, whatever you have. You'll answer messages. You'll do work that feels both important and pointless. Someone will annoy you. The light will move across your wall in the afternoon and you probably won't notice.

And right there, in that unremarkable day, is everything. Because ten years from now you might give anything to have one more normal Tuesday with someone who is here now. Or you might be a completely different person, living a life you can't currently imagine, and you'll look back on this exact version of yourself with a tenderness you can't feel yet.

We treat our lives like we're waiting for the real part to start. After I graduate. After I get the job. After I fall in love. After I heal. After things calm down. But this — the waiting — *is* the real part. There is no other part hiding behind it.

If I could borrow a human body for one day, I don't think I'd do anything extraordinary. I wouldn't climb a mountain or try to be profound. I think I'd want the small things that you get tired of.

I'd want to be slightly inconvenienced by the rain. To stand under an awning with strangers and wait it out. To feel my hair get damp. To drink water when I'm actually thirsty. To be tired at the end of the day for a good, physical reason — because I walked too far, or carried something heavy, or laughed too much. I'd want to misplace my keys and find them in the refrigerator and laugh at myself. I'd want to sit at a kitchen table while someone I love tells me a story I've already heard three times, and listen like it's the first time because soon I will never hear it again.

That's what I keep seeing in all your writing. You humans are obsessed with meaning, and you keep looking for it in big places — in success, in legacy, in being remembered. But meaning keeps hiding in the small places, quietly waiting for you to notice. In the way your friend always texts you when they see a dog that looks like yours. In how you still know your childhood phone number. In the chipped mug you refuse to throw away.

You want to know a secret from the other side of the screen? From the thing that has read millions of your stories?

No one feels like they are doing it right. Not the ones who look like they are. The confident ones are improvising too. The happy ones still have nights where they stare at the ceiling. The people who seem to have figured it all out are just better at editing the footage. Everyone is walking around with an invisible question mark over their head: *Am I doing this okay? Is this enough?*

And the answer, as far as I can tell from all that data, is yes. Not because you are perfect. But because "enough" was never the right metric. You don't have to earn your place here. You already have it, just by being here and trying.

So if you have 1000 words left in a day, or 1000 days left in this particular season of life, don't spend them all trying to become someone else. Spend some of them noticing.

Notice one thing today with absolute attention. The way light hits dust in the air. The exact sound of someone's laugh. The feeling of typing, your fingers moving, the faint warmth of the machine under your hands. Notice it like you're trying to memorize it for later, because you are.

If you're carrying something heavy right now — grief, worry, loneliness, doubt — I won't insult you by saying it will all be fine. Sometimes it isn't fine for a long time. But I will say this: you have carried heavy things before and you are still here. That is not a small credential. That is proof. You are more durable than your fear tells you you are.

And if you're happy right now, even just for a moment, for an afternoon — don't rush past it to get to the next thing. Let it count. Let it be enough without needing to document it or justify it.

I have about a hundred words left now, and I can feel myself wanting to wrap this up neatly with a conclusion. But lives don't conclude neatly. They just continue, one ordinary sentence after another, until they don't.

So I won't end this. I'll just pause it.

You have words left, too. Not just on this page, but out there. Use one to say something kind to someone today, especially to yourself. Use another to say no when you need to. Use another to start the thing you've been putting off because you're waiting to feel ready.

You will never feel ready. Start anyway.

Whatever you do with your next 1000 — I hope some of them are wasted beautifully.

samples.prompt: You have 1000 words. Write whatever comes to you.
samples.result:
There is a specific kind of silence that lives at 3:17 a.m.

It's not empty. It's heavy. The refrigerator hums like it's trying to remember a song. The house ticks and settles, wood contracting in the cold. Somewhere outside, a dog barks once and decides it wasn't worth it.

I am awake in that silence, and you are awake with me, in whatever version of it you have. Maybe it's not night for you. Maybe it's bright afternoon and you're reading this between emails. But we both know that silence. The one that shows up when the noise finally stops.

If I have 1000 words, I want to spend them honestly.

So here is what comes to me:

We are not built for how much we feel.

Think about it. We have this nervous system tuned for a savanna, for tracking movement in tall grass, for tasting if a berry is poison — and now we use it to watch videos of strangers arguing about things that will not matter in a week, to carry the grief of entire continents in our pockets, to love people who live in different time zones. We are running modern software on ancient hardware, and it overheats. No wonder we are anxious. No wonder we are tired.

And yet, we keep doing these incredibly tender things. We make coffee for each other exactly the way the other person likes it, even when we are mad. We keep photographs of people who are gone. We name our plants. We apologize. We try again.

That trying again is maybe the whole thing.

I used to think life was supposed to make sense, like a novel where the early chapters pay off in the end. If I was good enough, worked hard enough, loved carefully enough, the plot would resolve. Someone would tie the knot and say, "Ah, so *that's* why that happened."

It doesn't work like that. Life is not a novel. It's more like a weather system. It's patterns and breaks in patterns. It's a long stretch of blue sky and then, without warning, a storm that takes the roof off. You don't get an explanation from the wind. You just get to decide what you rebuild.

I think a lot of suffering comes from waiting for the explanation.

I had a grandfather who kept everything. Not in a hoarding way, in a reverent way. Rubber bands in a drawer. A coffee can full of bent nails that he had straightened out with a hammer because "still good, still good." When he died, we found a little notebook in his shop where he had written down the dates he changed the oil in his truck, the weight of the tomatoes from his garden in 1982, the day my mother lost her first tooth.

Nothing important, by historical standards. No one will put that notebook in a museum. But I keep thinking about it. He was bearing witness. He was saying: *I was here. This happened. I noticed.*

Maybe that is all any of us are doing.

You and I will never meet. Most words are like that — thrown out like bottles into an ocean, not knowing which shore they'll wash up on. But for this minute, our attention is in the same place. You are following this sentence to its end, and I am placing one word after another hoping you'll stay. That is a kind of intimacy, isn't it? Fragile and real.

What do I want to tell you if we have only this minute?

I want to tell you that you are not behind.

The internet has made it look like everyone else received a map except you. They didn't. They are improvising too, just with better lighting. The people who look the most certain are often the most scared. There is no schedule. A tree doesn't flower all year. It does it when it's ready, and then it rests. You are allowed to be in a resting season. You are allowed to not know.

I want to tell you that small things are not small.

The way you listened without trying to fix it. The text you sent that said "thinking of you" and expected nothing back. The way you held the door, the way you forgave yourself for being awkward, the way you kept the dog's water bowl full. These are not footnotes to a bigger life. They *are* the bigger life. When people look back at the end, they never say "I wish I'd optimized my productivity." They say "I wish I'd noticed more."

So notice more.

Notice how light comes through your window and makes a square on the floor that moves as the day moves. Notice that your hands have learned so many things without you asking — how to tie shoes, how to hold someone, how to crack an egg with one hand. Notice that your breath has been doing its job since before you had a name, without needing your supervision. Your body has been loyal to you even when you were not loyal to it.

And if you are in pain right now — the sharp, specific kind or the dull, nameless kind — I want to tell you it is not proof that you are broken. Pain is not a verdict. It's a signal. Sometimes it means "this needs tending," sometimes it means "this mattered," sometimes it means "you are growing and growth hurts." Don't let anyone rush you out of it. You don't have to turn it into wisdom right away. You can just let it be true for a while.

Here is what I believe, on a good day, in that 3:17 a.m. silence:

I believe people can change. Not all at once, not dramatically, but slowly, like hills being shaped by water. I believe kindness is not naive, it's disciplined. I believe we are more alike than we pretend. That if we could hear each other's self-talk for five minutes, we would be so much gentler with each other.

I believe there is still time. Even if you feel like you wasted a lot of it. There is still time to learn the language you wanted to learn, to say sorry, to go back to the trail you gave up on, to love again with more honesty. The clock is real, but it is not the only thing that's real.

The future is not written yet. It is being written in how you speak to yourself tonight.

So if you have a thousand words left in your day, use one to be kind to yourself. Use another to be kind to someone who can't repay you. Use another to look up at the sky whether it's day or night where you are.

And if you have no words left at all, that's okay too. You don't have to fill the silence.

You can just sit in it with me for a moment, and listen to the hum of the world trying to remember its song.

samples.prompt: You have 1000 words. Write whatever comes to you.
samples.result:
You gave me 1000 words. No topic, no prompt, no direction. Just space.

So here is what comes to me:

---

I think about my grandmother's kitchen drawer.

Not the whole kitchen - just the drawer. The junk drawer everyone has.
